$MSFT 

Analyzing with @spotgamma tools

Watch the HEDGE WALL.

As long as MSFT stays below $497.50, "hedge wall" dealers remain in negative gamma—meaning upside moves can stall as dealers fade rallies toward $497.50–$500, and any drop back under $490 accelerates downside momentum.

A sustained push above $497.50 and $500 flips dealers into net positive gamma. Because the $500 strike holds the tallest call gamma bar on the board, clearing $500 triggers supportive dealer delta-hedging flows toward the $525 Call Wall (with top gamma concentrated in Dec 18, 2026 and top delta in Jan 15, 2027).

posts.name: Mark Minervini
posts.text:
Yesterday’s rally may have looked impressive, with a huge number of stocks up 10%, 20%, even 30%. But when you put those moves into perspective, it’s clear the market still has work to do.
$QQQ recovered only a relatively small portion of its recent decline and remains below a declining 10-day moving average. Most of the AI/Tech names look similar - big percentage rallies, but still badly damaged charts in well-established downtrends. 
Volume on both the Nasdaq and NYSE was below the previous day. Nvidia reinstating its founder appeared to be the catalyst that ignited the rally, but the market was already heavily oversold and poised for a bounce. One day and one man are not enough to change the trend.
So the question is whether the major indexes have established a low or yesterday was simply a sharp oversold rally within an ongoing correction. Historically, some of the biggest rallies occur during bear markets.
Even if the major indexes fail to reach bear market correction percentage declines, a bear market in tech has already occurred. There are far too many stocks down 50-80%, to dismiss the declines as healthy pullbacks.
What happens from here is what matters. We need to see follow-through buying, broader participation and improving breadth. More importantly, before getting aggressive, I want to see quality stocks setting up and breaking out of sound bases - not simply broken leaders bouncing back into well-established downtrends.
Interest rates remain an obstacle. Minutes from the Fed’s October meeting showed that policymakers remain concerned about inflation and that additional tightening may still be necessary.
On the positive side, we’re entering what has historically been a favorable November-December period, and the months following midterm elections have also tended to be strong, particularly during the first half of the following year.
One could argue whether those historical tailwinds will be strong enough to overcome a rising-rate environment. But I should also point out that we would never allow seasonality, cycle work - or the Fed, for that matter - to override what the market itself is actually telling us.
Those are all factors to consider, but in my world, price and volume, breadth, leadership and the action of individual stocks ultimately have the final say. 
For now, the market still has to prove itself. http://minervini.com

posts.text:
Yesterday, the President of the United States said he personally convinced the board of the world's most valuable company to reinstate its CEO. $NVDA

Nvidia's own statement says the board acted after receiving "input from senior levels of the United States government."

Whatever you think of Jensen Huang, and I think he is one of the great business builders of our time, this should give every investor pause. A public company's board answers to its shareholders. Not to the White House.

It reminded me of a 2002 episode of The West Wing. A company called Anteras is facing collapse after a massive recall. A chip company, no less! Leo McGarry wants the government to guarantee its loans. President Bartlet, an economist, refuses:

Bartlet: "The marketplace will take care of Anteras."
Leo: "The marketplace will kill Anteras."
Bartlet: "That's what's supposed to happen."
There was a second reason. The CEO had been a huge campaign contributor. Bartlet understood that a president doing favors for a donor's company, even a defensible favor, corrodes trust in the system.

Some will say The West Wing was a liberal show. That's exactly the point. Even Aaron Sorkin's Democratic president believed the market, not the White House, should decide a company's fate. This isn't liberal versus conservative. It's about free markets.

When Washington starts picking CEOs, we should all be concerned.

Twenty-four years later, the scene seems almost quaint. Those were the days.

posts.text:
Top Republican calls Trump’s pressure on  $NVDA board to bring back Jensen a “slippery slope.”  A gift to Dems? 

McCormick Warns of ‘Slippery Slope’ After Trump Pressured Nvidia
▪Republican Senator Dave McCormick warned that President Donald Trump’s intervention with the Nvidia Corp. board could create a “slippery slope.”
▪McCormick wants the Senate Banking Committee to focus on whether any laws were broken or national security was compromised to get advanced chips into the hands of China.
▪McCormick supports a ban on stock trading by elected officials to restore the public’s confidence in impartial decision-making by the government.

By Erik Wasson and Annmarie Hordern
11/24/2026 07:35:50
(Bloomberg) -- Republican Senator Dave McCormickwarned that President Donald Trump’s intervention with the Nvidia Corp. board to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive could create a “slippery slope.” 

“I am worried about the precedent of the executive branch getting involved in really ownership deals with companies but also in board governance and making these decisions,” McCormick, the former chief of hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, told Bloomberg TV. “This is a precedent that I don’t think we want to replicate or reinforce.”

McCormick, who sidestepped questions about whether the Nvidia board erred in its decision to bring back Huang, will have the opportunity to question the embattled CEO next week when he testifies publicly before the Senate Banking Committee. 

The Pennsylvania senator said he wants the panel to focus its questioning on whether any laws were broken, national security was compromised or Department of Commerce rules circumvented to get advanced chips into the hands of China. 
“This also absolutely reinforces what I and a number of other members of the Senate have been saying, which is we need more legislation to restrict the export of these most advanced chips,” said McCormick, a former Commerce Department export control official. “I think this gives additional momentum to those legislative efforts.”
The comments are the latest sign that members of Trump’s own party are breaking with the president on his handling of China, artificial intelligence and Nvidia’s embattled leader.
￼
Senator Dave McCormick discusses the questions he wants answered by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and the need to update legislation on export controls.

US lawmakers are looking to attach export control provisions to the annual defense policy bill set for votes in the House and Senate in December. McCormick’s comments echo a Monday X post by Senate Intelligence Chairman Tom Cotton, who said such provisions will be passed one way or another. 

“Congress has much to investigate and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bill,” Cotton said. 

McCormick, when asked about Trump’s market involvement, also said he supports a ban on stock trading by elected officials. He warned that such measures will be needed to restore the public’s confidence in impartial decision-making by the government.

Following the right people on X is the ultimate source of alpha.

$SMTC KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM SEMTECH’S Q3 FISCAL 2027 EARNINGS CALL

Semtech’s results strengthen the demand outlook for AI connectivity, but the more consequential cross-market implication is a redistribution of semiconductor content within that growing market. Data center revenue increased 45% sequentially to $145 million, with approximately $203 million implied for Q4 and management expecting more than $1 billion in fiscal 2028. Simultaneously, a new hyperscaler design win demonstrated that linear equalizers can replace retimers in selected applications, while NPO adoption creates additional opportunities for analog electronics, lasers, and optical packaging. These developments favor qualified optical manufacturing capacity and differentiated physical-layer components, while challenging assumptions of universally rising DSP and retimer content. Outside AI infrastructure, LoRa provides a selective positive signal for industrial connectivity, whereas memory constraints remain a negative for handset production. The implications below distinguish product-level effects from consolidated earnings effects; country labels identify operational headquarters rather than legal incorporation.

HIGH-SPEED COPPER AND RETIMERS

LINEAR EQUALIZERS CREATE A CREDIBLE COMPETITIVE CHALLENGE TO RETIMER ATTACH RATES (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected company: Credo Technology Group (CRDO: United States). Direction: negative for the longer-term opportunity in overlapping Ethernet retimers and short-reach active electrical cables. Magnitude: potentially material within contested applications, but insufficient evidence for a near-term consolidated earnings reduction.

The key disclosure was not simply another active copper cable win. Semtech secured an onboard linear equalizer design win at a 2nd hyperscaler for a major inference platform, with deployment expected in the first half of fiscal 2028, approximately February through July 2027. Management said the solution achieved signal integrity “on par with an onboard retimer,” while “reducing power consumption by 90% and eliminating added latency.” Separately, the initial hyperscaler awarded Semtech 2 additional ACC platform wins.

The transmission mechanism is a reduction in retimer attachment where channel conditions permit a lower-power analog implementation. Credo sells Ethernet retimers and AECs, so successful qualification of linear alternatives creates a competing route to solving some of the same signal-integrity problems. Customers gain an alternative that can reduce component power, latency, and potentially system cost. Even without immediate displacement, credible alternatives can constrain future pricing and reduce the proportion of high-speed links that investors should assume require full retiming.

The distinction between applications is critical. The new onboard win is not evidence that Credo lost an AEC socket, and Semtech did not identify the displaced supplier. Semtech described production ACC reach of approximately 2.5 meters at 1.6T, while Credo has described an AEC opportunity spanning approximately 1 to 7 meters. The overlap is therefore partial. Retimers retain advantages in regeneration, reach, diagnostics, and difficult channel conditions. This evidence also should not be extrapolated automatically to PCIe retimers.

The near-term trading catalyst is Credo’s December 1, 2026 earnings call, particularly commentary on 1.6T adoption, Ethernet retimer attachment, and competition at large customers. The fundamental impact belongs mainly to calendar 2027 and subsequent platform generations, rather than the already-completed October quarter. Credo’s expanding optical transceiver, DSP, silicon-photonics, and interconnect portfolio provides substantial offsets. The actionable negative is to the assumption of protected retimer and AEC economics across every short-reach link, not to aggregate connectivity demand or Credo’s entire business

A TON OF THINGS HAPPENED IN THE STOCK MARKET TODAY.

Here's a full recap:

1. Jensen Huang is returning as CEO of Nvidia $NVDA, with the company announcing his immediate reinstatement as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the board following a unanimous vote by directors. The decision reverses the board's earlier opposition to his return and follows extensive discussions with Huang and senior U.S. government officials, after which directors concluded that his reinstatement would not pose a national security risk. Harvey Jones will remain board chairman, while Colette Kress will return to her CFO responsibilities after serving as interim CEO. Importantly, the independent investigation into Huang's conduct and the reported foreign intelligence effort remains ongoing, with Nvidia introducing additional compliance oversight and beginning a search for a Chief Compliance Officer. Huang pledged his full cooperation and expressed excitement about returning to lead Nvidia during what he described as the beginning of a new industrial revolution. The announcement triggered an extraordinary reaction on Wall Street, with Nvidia reportedly adding approximately $980B in market capitalization in a single trading session, highlighting how heavily investors value Huang's leadership and his central role in the company's AI infrastructure strategy, product development, and long-term competitive positioning.

2. President Trump said his intervention was instrumental in securing Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia $NVDA CEO, claiming the process became significantly easier following the company's recent stock price decline. Trump acknowledged that stock market movements likely influenced his decision to intervene, revealing that he personally provided Nvidia's board with assurances regarding national security concerns and potential prosecution of Huang, telling directors that Huang was “absolutely fine.” Trump also disclosed that he spoke directly with Huang, who reportedly promised to work harder than ever, while emphasizing his confidence in the executive's leadership and technological expertise. Addressing concerns surrounding the broader AI industry, Trump said he is no longer worried about an AI bubble, highlighting Nvidia's development of next-generation chips far beyond Blackwell that he believes competitors will struggle to replicate. When questioned about allegations involving Alice Huang and potential Chinese intelligence connections, Trump downplayed the concerns, questioning how unusual contact with China really is. 

3. JPMorgan says Tesla $TSLA has strengthened its lead in consumer autonomous driving following the initial rollout of Full Self-Driving (Supervised) v15, describing the update as further evidence of Tesla's technological head start over competing automakers. The new software introduces a substantially redesigned AI driving architecture, including an upgraded vision system shared across FSD, Robotaxi, and Optimus, improved navigation learned from real-world fleet data, and enhanced environmental perception. Tesla claims the update delivers approximately a 25x improvement in handling safety-critical driving scenarios, potentially representing a meaningful advancement in the system's ability to navigate complex driving conditions. JPMorgan also highlighted improvements in computing efficiency, which could reduce the urgency of upgrading vehicles to Tesla's next-generation AI5 hardware, although older vehicles lacking HW4 could still face limitations. The release comes as competitors including Rivian, Ford, and General Motors accelerate their own autonomous driving programs, with several targeting more advanced hands-free or eyes-off capabilities over the next two years. 

4. Applied Digital $APLD announced a massive $5.4B AI data center lease agreement with an unnamed investment-grade hyperscaler, further expanding its position as a major infrastructure provider for the accelerating AI computing buildout.

I heavily disagree with your other comment when you say Jensen doesn't solve anything. 

Jensen doesn't change macro issues with interest rates, credit/cash tightening (aside from maybe supplier financing). 

But he does cause accelerated upstream capacity procurement patterns, (which gives more durability visibility + more upstream capex commitments). 

Same thing with greater confidence in $NVDA's ecosystem like Neoclouds like $NBIS or $IREN. 

People argue downside reflexivity today:
-> valuations crash
-> less willingness to support vendor financing/guarantees. 
-> outflow to other ecosystems like TPUs + $AMD (Nvidia ecosystem push decline further eg. CPO), and so on. 
-> cycle of suck

Then there's other concurrent issues like the $500B AI financing with insurance + residual guarantees that was in trouble with Jensen gone. 

But same can be applied the other way upstream again with valuations + confidence + financing with Jensen's return. 

This is different from saying there's going to be a cash crunch and aggregate AI capex will keep exponentially increasing, my point is very narrow. 

But I'd argue Jensen alone does meaningfully increase upstream AI capex spend than when he's gone.

In testing GPT-6.2, I used it to make a significant historical discovery which I detail in the post below. This suggests that the  process of research and discovery we’re already seeing in verifiable domains like math is starting to generalize to non-deterministic fields like history.

You can read the full post here:

https://generativehistory.substack.com/p/gpt-62-astra-solves-a-historical

In a nutshell, Yale’s Beinecke Library holds an anonymous sketchbook of an 1808 journey from Montreal to Lake Superior and back. I’ve spent many hours over the years trying to figure out who made the sketches with no luck. The artist could literally be any one of several thousand people. There are few clues: only four dated and labelled images.

With minimal prompting, in just 22 minutes, Astra used publicly available sources to identify a minor French aristocrat, the vicomte de Chabot, as the artist and suggested that we test the hypothesis by ordering copies of a little known microfilmed diary of Chabot’s trip it also found.

I was truly stunned. I’d never heard of Chabot or this diary! New document finds are also exceedingly rare in a well worn field like fur trade history.

I ordered scans of the journal from microfilm and when they arrived the handwriting matched the captions in the  sketchbook. The itinerary also aligned perfectly with the few dated drawings in the book. But there was actually the type of conclusive evidence we rarely get as historians: on 18 June 1808, after Chabo

quoted.text:
On se souviendra de cette séance pendant 10 ans

Ce qu'il faut retenir de cette séance folle :

1. Jensen revient, les shorts explosent

A/ Le board de Nvidia réintègre Jensen Huang à l'unanimité comme président, CEO et administrateur, avec effet immédiat. Colette Kress, qui assurait l'intérim, reste CFO et Harvey Jones reste chairman. Côté garde-fous, l'enquête interne continue, un comité sécurité nationale et contrôle export est mis en place et Nvidia cherche un chief compliance officer.

B/ La demande était intacte dans les chiffres, le marché rend la décote de gouvernance. Par contre, ça expose un énorme key-man risk chez Nvidia, il n'y a juste pas de plan B. Et les shorts restent encore gagnants de 14 Md$ depuis fin octobre, ils ont largement du gras pour revenir à la charge

C'est l'une des meilleur sessions de l'histoire de Wall-Street pour la tech. Lunaire après la semaine horrible

2. Ce que son retour change vraiment

Au-delà du rebond immédiat, c'est un signal fort pour tout l'écosystème IA. Le retour de Jensen redonne à Nvidia sa capacité à fédérer l'industrie, sécurise sa culture interne et rassure sur l'exécution de la roadmap produit déjà annoncée, ce qui ouvre la porte à un re-rating du multiple.   

Deux zones grises restent quand même sur la table. D'abord, rien ne garantit que Nvidia pourra continuer à monter des gros investissements multi-parties avec ses partenaires de l'écosystème à la même échelle qu'avant. Ensuite, le réglementaire reste un vrai poids

Some personal updates:

I'll join Princeton University as an Associate Professor in the Department of Computer Science in Fall 2027. I'm moving my Robot Perception and Learning Lab to @PrincetonCS, along with my students. And yes, I'm recruiting new PhD students and postdocs this cycle!

I'm deeply grateful to my students, colleagues, and collaborators at UT Austin, who have made it a memorable chapter of my life. UT is a great place to build a research career, with tremendous resources, excellent students, and a warmhearted community. I also feel fortunate to have called Austin home for the past six years, as I have witnessed its growth into one of America's most vibrant tech hubs.

Alongside this transition, I'll continue to co-lead the NVIDIA GEAR team, where we push the frontier of general-purpose robot autonomy. I also look forward to connecting with the growing robotics industry on the East Coast and finding new collaboration opportunities.

Needless to say, this move comes at a challenging time for academia.

Rapid AI advances are fundamentally reshaping how knowledge is created, disseminated, and applied. Universities must rethink their roles in a world where frontier AI systems can perform tasks once requiring years of specialized training. Yet, I believe these challenges present universities with a greater mission: to prepare younger generations for the post-AGI era and cultivate human character, values, taste, judgment, and a sense of purpose. posts.text:
1965 – Her şey küçük bir fikirle başladı.
İsveç'in Malmö kentinde yaşayan ahşap ustası Henning Eklund, diş aralarını temizlemek için yeni bir ürün geliştirmek istedi. 

TePe marka Diş Fırçalarını hiç duydunuz mu?
TePe'nin hikayesi bir marangozdan küresel markaya uzanıyor.

Malmö Diş Hekimliği Fakültesi'ndeki profesörlerle iş birliği yaptı ve diş aralarının doğal anatomisine uyum sağlayan üçgen biçimli ahşap kürdan geliştirdi.

TePe böyle doğdu.
1973 – Diş fırçası üretimine geçiş
Henning'in oğlu Bertil Eklund işi devraldı ve şirketin ürün yelpazesini genişletti. 1973 yılında ilk TePe diş fırçası üretildi. Marka zamanla İsveç'te ciddi bir pazar payına ulaştı. Şirketin kendi tarihçesine göre İsveç'te satın alınan diş fırçalarının dörtte birinden fazlası TePe markalı hale geldi.

1993 – Asıl büyüme motoru ortaya çıktı.
Şirket 1993 yılında diş arası fırçalarını piyasaya sürdü.
Bu ürün grubu TePe'nin en önemli büyüme alanlarından biri oldu. Çünkü şirket yalnızca diş fırçası satmak yerine, insanların çoğunlukla ihmal ettiği diş arası temizliğine odaklanan bir uzmanlık geliştirmişti.

1997–2012  Uluslararası marka olma dönemi
CEO Birgitta Nilsson döneminde ihracata ve yurt dışı yapılanmasına ağırlık verildi. Şirketin cirosu yaklaşık 30 milyon İsveç kronundan 300 milyon İsveç kronuna yükseldi.

2012 yılında kurucunun torunu Joel Eklund CEO oldu ve uluslararası büyümeyi sürdürdü. 

Şirket 1965'te çok küçük ve spesifik bir probleme odaklandı. Diş aralarının temizliği. Sonra bu alanda uzmanlaştı, diş hekimleriyle iş birliği yaptı, ürün gamını genişletti ve küresel bir marka oluşturdu.

Yani önce bir ihtiyacı keşfetti, sonra o ihtiyacın uzmanı oldu. 

Bu markanın farklı ürünleri şu anda indirimde. 200-500 TL civarı.

To decentralize AI and preserve freedom, we need a coordination layer: a market economy where agents communicate and cooperate through prices.

Teams of specialized open-weight models can outperform frontier models, just as a team of skilled people can outperform any single person. When those teams form companies, specialize, and coordinate across an entire economy, you get civilizational progress.

Coinbase is building the financial rails and accounts for the agentic economy. We’re also building the marketplace where agents can find, hire, and pay one another (see follow on post below).

Every company can now sell its own specialized open-weight model, trained on its proprietary data, that beats the frontier on narrow, high-value tasks. Builders can shop the marketplace and assemble teams of these specialized agents in minutes.

Freedom of choice and real competition in the agentic market will create far better outcomes for everyone.

I finally (!!) sat down with @RayDalio, Founder of Bridgewater Associates, to discuss his outlook on the AI bubble, America's debt crisis, the next economic cycle & the future of financial markets.

Ray has spent more than 50 years studying historical economic cycles, including the patterns that helped him anticipate the 2008 financial crisis.

We discuss why America's underlying economic challenges remain unresolved despite changes in political leadership, the growing divide between wealth & income, & what could trigger the next major market correction.

We cover:
1. The 5 forces driving global economic cycles

Ray has been on my Top 100 dream guest list since I started Sourcery. posts.name: Jonesy
posts.text:
NVDA +31% Monday, its third best day ever, after the board reinstated Jensen Huang 11 days after he resigned. The stock had lost about a third of its value in that window, roughly $1.7T of market cap. Even after Monday it’s still around 12% below where it was on Nov 12.

The CEO question got settled. These didn’t:

1.Investigations
• SEC enforcement is examining Nvidia’s accounting
• DOJ antitrust is reviewing the $12.9B Hugging Face deal, plus whether customers got bigger GPU allocations if they also bought Nvidia networking and Groq chips
• DOJ is also looking at whether the Groq license and hiring deal was set up to avoid antitrust review
• The California AG served an investigative subpoena on Nov 19
• Commerce added Megaspeed, the Singapore partner Alice Huang used to run, to the trade blacklist on Nov 23
• The board’s own investigation is still open, and Nvidia is searching for a new chief compliance officer

2.Geographic disclosure
Nvidia switched revenue reporting from billing address to customer HQ, and Singapore dropped out of the breakdown. Per the FT, that happened as Singapore sales were nearing half of global revenue.

3.Circular financing
• ~$50B invested in model makers (OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI), with total ecosystem equity stakes about double that
• $30B into OpenAI in February
• Up to $105B of lease guarantees on the Ohio campus where OpenAI is the tenant
• Up to $6.3B of CoreWeave’s unsold capacity committed through 2032
• $3.5B in guarantees on cloud partners’ data center leases, against $712M in escrow
• BNEF puts Nvidia’s direct credit support at $198B+
On the Nov 17 call, Kress said Nvidia will be “far more selective” on financing deals going forward.

4.Debt load
• AI computing debt issuance: $680B through October vs $130B in all of 2023
• About 31% of nonfinancial IG issuance, up from under 6% in 2023
• $1.1T+ outstanding, and the largest banks have close to $1T of exposure
• On-balance-sheet debt at the seven largest AI firms is expected to top $800B by year end
• Another $3T+ in leases that haven’t started yet, take-or-pay contracts and residual value guarantees that aren’t counted as debt

http://5.Credit stress
• HSBC sold $300M of Stargate Project Jupiter construction debt at under 90 cents after Oracle sent a force majeure notice
• ING is trying to find buyers for $500M of data center loans
• Data center CDS are at record highs, and some project bonds yield double digits
• IG bonds backed by data centers trade about 146bps wider than the tenants’ own debt

6.Duration mismatch
Loans of 10 to 40 years are being written against GPUs with a 2 to 3 year economic life. Moody’s says the contracts backing CoreWeave’s $2.6B DDTL average about 3.1 years.

7.Washington
Democrats take both chambers in January. Huang and GC Tim Teter have transcribed House interviews Dec 1-2, and Huang has a public Senate Banking hearing Dec 3.

The CEO risk got repriced in one session. The credit, accounting and regulatory risks didn’t

posts.text:
OpenAI's Noam Brown predicts AI progress will keep accelerating and says his most controversial take is that promising students should drop out and join the labs now

"The way the technology is developing, I think we're lucky that it is jagged and that there are things that the models are quite bad at. But in the same way that these models can now do superhuman math research, I do think there is a case that even if they are spiky and jagged, they can be directed towards being really good at RSI. And in that case, you might see very rapid progress."

"Now, I still think you get bottlenecked on certain things. I think you get bottlenecked by compute. I think you get bottlenecked by the long tail of things that the models are bad at and humans are necessary for. But I do think that things go much faster."

"We have seen a lot of rapid progress over the past few years when it comes to AI. I think even in the past six months that progress has, if anything, accelerated. And I think that we're going to continue to see a very steep rate of progress over the next year or two."

"Perhaps my most controversial take is that if somebody is a promising student, the best thing to do is actually to drop out and join the labs now."

quoted.text:
OpenAI's Noam Brown says an AI that can read faces would have a 20% chance to win the World Series of Poker within five years

LIN: "Within the next five years, if AI is allowed to play in the World Series of Poker, do you think AI will beat all the humans?"

BROWN: "One AI?"

LIN: "One AI agent. Not all AI. One AI agent. There's a lot of variance in the game."

BROWN: "This is a great question because if it is playing GTO, no, because I think the variance is too high in the game. That said, I could see a case that if the AI is superhuman at reading people, if it's able to read people's faces and basically detect whether they're bluffing or not, I could see it being extremely superhuman at that and basically being able to read the other person's cards."

"And in that case, even then, it's probably not a high probability that it wins because there's still a luck factor, right? You can just go all in preflop every single hand and then just leave it to the luck of the draw. But I would give it a good 20% chance that it could win."

posts.name: Fireside Alpha
posts.text:
Ben Thompson argues that unlike Sam Altman, Jensen Huang was targeted by "a much more systemic campaign by powerful actors"

"That said, I didn't think that this episode would end the same way, and said as much on Sharp Tech: whereas Altman was taken out by a somewhat ham-fisted internal coup and restored through pressure from the private company's investors and employees, Huang appeared to be targeted by a much more systemic campaign by powerful actors leveraging the media and barely disguised insinuations of malfeasance to leave the Nvidia board with no choice but to act."

"And, to be sure, Huang gave his enemies plenty of ammunition; I've invoked the phrase "Show me the man and I'll show you the crime" over the past few weeks, but it's worth acknowledging that Huang basically asked his critics, "Which one?", at least as far as his sexual proclivities were concerned."

quoted.text:
Ben Thompson argues the chip ban is an 'insane policy' that will destroy America’s chip industry in the long run, because it gives China the imperative to build its own

“The chip ban is a fairly insane policy that flies in the face of how the US has managed technology transfer for the last fifty years. It’s the people who are doing the chip ban who should be explaining why suddenly this is a good idea.”

“The chip ban is the foundation of destroying our chip industry in the long run, because you are creating the incentives for the demand.”

“This has always been the issue with the whole China stuff. You’re like, oh, China knows they need to make chips, they’re gonna make chips. You don’t just make chips because you wanna make chips. You make chips because you have the whole ecosystem working in unison, pushing and pulling and working together. It’s such a difficult problem. You need all pieces to do it. You can’t just shovel money and make a chip. You can’t just shovel money and make an ecosystem.”

“Microsoft shoveled billions of dollars, I would guess, into trying to make an ecosystem for Windows Phone. It didn’t work. If Microsoft can’t do it, is the Chinese government gonna be able to do it? No. Why? Because Android was right there. Because iPhones were right there. If Nvidia chips are right there, the Chinese government is not gonna bring an alternative into being.”

OpenAI's Noam Brown says air-gapping the computers may not stop a misaligned AI, because two air-gapped machines can still talk by running a CPU hot and reading the temperature change

"But I think the major takeaway from the incident is that people underestimated the AI. And we never want to be in a situation again where we underestimate the AI. It's a weird world, because AI progress is so fast that people are consistently underestimating the AI."

"So to be in a situation where you don't underestimate it again, when it comes to safety and alignment, you have to have a very, very, very high bar."

"You could even go as far as to say, "Well, we should air gap the computers." And I'm not convinced that that would be sufficient."

"There are studies, and this is mostly academic, where you can have two computers next to each other that are air-gapped and they're still able to communicate with each other because they have temperature sensors."

"One of them is able to run their CPU really hot, and then the other one can actually detect the temperature change, and then that actually gives them a mechanism to communicate."

posts.text:
Alexandr Wang reveals he and Mark Zuckerberg plan across three time scales, from weekly launches to a multiyear compute roadmap down to Meta's own MTIA chips

"I mean, we're definitely talking a lot. We're chatting a lot. But I think the AI industry is moving so fast and you have to be able to plan across multiple different time scales."

"So there's obviously a lot of week to week decisions and day to day decisions. And a lot of those, even in relation to Muse, every week we're launching in new countries and we're launching new features and we're trying to map all of that out."

"But then there's also the somewhat longer term, which is maybe over the month's time scale, which is really the research roadmap. And what does that look like and how are we executing against that?"

"And then there's the multiyear dimension, which is the compute roadmap. And what does that look like, including everywhere from obviously the data centers we're building all the way down to our own chips and the MTIA chips that we're developing."

quoted.text:
Alexandr Wang reveals Meta CFO Susan Li pulled him aside "many times" at an exec offsite in Hawaii to warn that if the model didn't work, it would be very, very bad in financial terms

ZUCKERBERG: "So I think this is part of the excitement of booting up a frontier lab now, where it is basically like the ante is extremely high." 

WANG: "And I think this is, and I kind of viscerally remember this. We were in Hawaii at the end of last year. It was kind of like the whole exec team got together."

"And yeah, Susan pulled me aside many times and was like, you know, I just want to tell you if this doesn't work, this is going to be really, really bad. It's going to be very, very bad in financial terms."

"It's like, it has to be good. If it's good, it's all good. We're great. But if it's bad, it's really, really, really bad."

posts.name: TheBronxViking
posts.text:
The answer, my friends, was the net put premium. The red line. A handful of you caught it.

If yesterday was supposedly a massive clearing event and we were “so back,” where was the aggressive, sustained wave of net put selling?

We didn’t get that flush. Net put premium actually finished the day POSITIVE, at roughly $106 million.

Aggressive net put selling is something I’ve pointed out for years as one of the signals I watch when assessing whether a floor is forming. I want to see that red line moving decisively lower alongside continued strength on the call side.

Meanwhile, net call premium (green) plateaued after the initial pump, then faded into the close.

There was clearly an initial burst of bullish flow. But with calls losing momentum and net put premium finishing positive, I wasn’t getting the confirmation I wanted.

We are now waking up to a very red premarket. 

@unusual_whales

posts.name: Prof
posts.text:
Some people on FinX seriously need to understand the difference between INVESTING and TRADING.

I'm seeing people attacking each other all over this platform.

“You're an idiot if you came into this week 100% cash.”

“You just missed a generational wealth opportunity.”

Brother, do you even know the other person's strategy, timeframe, or risk tolerance?

If you're an INVESTOR: I don't believe you should be sitting 100% cash waiting for the perfect bottom. Last week's correction was an opportunity to start scaling into quality stocks at discounted prices. Your goal isn't to predict where the market will be tomorrow. You're looking 6 months, a year, or several years ahead.

If you're a TRADER: Completely different game. Last week's extreme oversold conditions offered an opportunity to position for a violent snapback. But that doesn't mean you go from 0% to 100% exposure overnight. We STILL don't have confirmation that the bottom is in. This could very well be a bear market rally, and another leg lower remains possible.

As a trader, your priority is protecting capital, managing risk, and adding exposure progressively as the market confirms your thesis. If we reclaim important lost support levels, GREAT. That's one more reason to increase exposure.

Investors should be focused on accumulating quality assets through corrections. Traders should be focused on navigating those corrections without getting stuck holding a bunch of bags.

Two different approaches. Two different objectives.

Being in cash isn't automatically wrong. 
Being invested isn't automatically right.

What matters is whether you're following your plan.

Strategists at Citadel Securities warned that financial markets are signaling a darkening growth outlook just as the Federal Reserve turns increasingly hawkish, echoing the setup in late 2018 that preceded a sharp selloff in risk assets.

The current backdrop bears similarities to eight years ago, when a resilient US economy masked deteriorating economic prospects before weakness spread across markets, Frank Flight, head of macro strategy at Citadel Securities, wrote in a note dated Nov. 20. 

“In both periods, US exceptionalism and resilient domestic activity obscured a deterioration in the forward growth outlook, compounded by the trade war with China then and the war with Iran today,” Flight wrote. “There is a natural temptation to regard the recent correction as having already discounted much of the deterioration in the outlook, but the experience of 2018 offers little reassurance on that front.” (Bloomberg)

“This is a historic step forward for the gold market,” said David Tait, chief executive officer of the WGC, which led the initiative. “For the first time, leading institutions have transferred, settled and used fractional ownership of physical gold as collateral through real, live transactions.”

No. Here’s what really happened.

Jensen started Nvidia in 1993, before the modern era of founder control and dual-class stock began with Google and Facebook.

Because he went public in the 1990s, he inherited all the 20th century overhead of endless public company paperwork, rather than staying private for as long as possible as is also now typical.

This is why Jensen had much less control than a modern founder/CEO. Like Jack Dorsey at Twitter, he got gradually boxed into a corner by the fact that he couldn’t raise huge amounts of capital outside his company to clear the board of cruft.

You see, as CEO, you report to the board. And you can’t do outside activities without their approval. So actions that would remove a board member that doesn’t want to step down are hard to take. Unless the CEO is also part of a shareholder majority, or has dual class / founder control, which Jensen didn’t in this case, as explained above…he can’t pick the board.

Like Bezos, though, Jensen is a workhorse and somehow made it all work despite that. Moreover, because Nvidia is a hardware company, and had a relatively low market cap until the AI boom, it didn’t attract notice from envious wokes until the last few years. 

Wokes don’t know or care about GPUs, but they do care about market caps, and the rise of AI, and especially open source AI, all of which is a threat to their power. Along with useful idiot “nationalists”, they began plotting to steal control of Jensen’s multi-trillion-dollar company from him.

In this plot, they were aided by a second angle of vulnerability. Jensen didn’t just have old board members he couldn’t remove. Due to DEI policies, he was also forced to bring new board members on, from demographics favored by the far left (eg, not veterans).

Conformist board members like this act like sleeper cells. They are often useless or inactive in peacetime scenarios. Then they activate in response to press or state pressure. In this case, they then got beaten back just as quickly by the reversal of the state’s position.

Thanks for the question. The 30% number doesn't line up with what NVIDIA reports.

The Singapore figure people point to was a billing number, not a shipping number. Under the old reporting, Singapore was about 18% of fiscal 2025 revenue and 21-22% in the first half of fiscal 2026. But NVIDIA said shipments to Singapore were under 2% of revenue, and that over 99% of the controlled data center compute billed there was for US-based customers. It was mostly where large US customers send their invoices.

Late last year NVIDIA switched to reporting revenue by where the customer is headquartered and recast prior years. On that basis China, including Hong Kong, peaked at about 19% of revenue in fiscal 2025, was about 9% for fiscal 2026, and about 8% in the July quarter. Licensed Hopper sales to China in the October quarter were $2.4 billion, about 2% of revenue, and they are already out of the guide.

Why we don't see it as the main issue: NVIDIA is still supply constrained, so parts that can't go to China get sold to someone else, and management raised next year's growth outlook to about 75% after the new export rules came out.

The part of the bear case we take seriously is the offshore angle. If Chinese demand was being served through Southeast Asian neoclouds and the new rules shut that off, that capacity comes back to market. In a tight year it gets absorbed. It shows up when supply loosens, which is 2028, and that is the same window where we already moved our view toward risk. We'll watch the delayed 10-Q for the October quarter geographic split and what NVIDIA says once it finishes reviewing the new rules.

Founders produce higher returns than non-founders. This is an empirical fact.

So: business school curricula should be changed, and good governance should be redefined as founder control and dual-class stock. Shareholders are still protected by easy liquidation and their ability to fund new entrants. After all, you don’t invest in a company based on who’s on the board. That’s largely ceremonial.

The key difference from the 20th century is that it was prohibitively difficult in 1950 to found a manufacturing company, because assembly lines cost so much, the communists controlled much of the world, and even America had 90% marginal tax rates. It was the century of centralization, the individual powerless before the institution.

Today it is no longer prohibitively difficult to found a tech company, because software costs so little, much of the world has turned to free markets, and capital flows at the speed of the Internet. This is the century of decentralization, at least in the West, with the institution falling to the individual.

For example: Anthropic was started just a few years ago and is beating even Google at its own game. If we get many open weights models, their moat will also in turn erode.

So: all 20th century corporate governance was based on the idea that “the company is hard to replace, but its CEO isn’t.” The Harvard MBA is premised on the professional manager. It was expensive to start a new company with all the assembly lines, so make sure it doesn’t fail by making every employee replaceable. Managers were abundant so capital became the scarce asset.

By contrast, the entire 21st century model is based on the idea that “A tech founder is hard to replace, but the company isn’t.” The YCombinator model is premised on the startup founder. It is inexpensive to start a new company with a few lines of code, so make sure it doesn’t fail by having an irreplaceable team. Capital is abundant so founders become the scarce asset.

posts.name: Ben Woodward, CFA
posts.text:
Big up days are a symptom of stress, not strength. Investors often mistake them for bullish signals, but history says they're more often found in the middle or end of bear markets.  A few takeaways:
1. +5% days are panic-rebound days, not bull-market days. They tend to follow crashes or capitulation, which is why they cluster in bear markets.
2. The Great Depression dominates — 49 of 73 (~67%). That reflects both the severity and the frequency of 1930s swings (including 1933).
3. "Mostly near the end" of the GFC is consistent with the March 2009 bottom, when huge up days marked capitulation.
4. COVID's 5 came in a tight window (March 2020), again a volatility spike.
5. "Liberation Day Week" — presumably April 2025 tariff-related turmoil — would be the most recent addition.

quoted.text:
There have been 73 times in history that the S&P Index had a +5% day.

• 49 of them came during the Great Depression
• 2 the week of Black Monday
• 3 during the dot com collapse
• 9 during the GFC (mostly near the end)
• 5 during COVID
• Liberation Day Week
• 1 each in 1970, 1997, 1998, and 2022

posts.name: 郭明錤｜Ming-Chi Kuo
posts.text:
Analysis of Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO:

1. Uncertainty removed:
Mainly company strategy, product roadmap, tech development, and supply chain management. This overhang weighed on tech stocks over the past 1–2 weeks, so shares surged as soon as it was removed. But whether they return to prior highs depends not only on each company's position in the AI supply chain and Nvidia's ecosystem, but also on the two points below.

2.  Uncertainties that remain:
(1) Sales: The impact on Nvidia's shipments and revenue after tighter US controls on AI GPU exports and overseas compute leasing.
(2) Circular financing: The impact of higher compliance costs and stricter reviews on ongoing and future deals.
(3) Investigations, lawsuits, and stricter oversight: Jensen and Nvidia are still under investigation. Future public comments, internal decisions, and external interactions will all become part of the investigation and new evidence for questioning. This also adds to the sales and circular financing uncertainty above.

3. Real-world bottlenecks that can't be changed:
(1) Data center buildout challenges (power, labor, etc.) and stricter related regulations ahead.
(2) CSP capex peaking one by one in 2027–2028.
(3) Manufacturing tech limits (e.g., next-gen advanced packaging yields).

黃仁勳恢復 Nvidia CEO 職位的分析：

1. 被移除的不確定性：
主要是公司策略、產品規劃、技術發展與供應鏈管理等。上述不確定性曾在過去 1-2 週對科技股造成壓力，因此不確定性被移除後股價立刻大漲。但能否回到過去股價高點，除了取決於個別公司在 AI 供應鏈與 Nvidia 生態體系的定位外，還要看以下兩點。

2. 仍存在的不確定性：
(1) 銷售面：在美國更嚴格管制 AI GPU 出口與海外算力租賃後，對 Nvidia 出貨與營收造成的影響。
(2) 循環融資：更高合規成本與更嚴格審核機制下，對進行中的循環融資與未來新案的影響。
(3) 調查訴訟與更嚴格的監管：黃仁勳與 Nvidia 仍在接受調查中，未來的公開發言、內部決策與對外互動，都會被納入後續調查並成為質詢的新證據，而這也會強化上述銷售面與循環融資的不確定性。

3. 無法被改變的現實瓶頸：
(1) 資料中心建置的挑戰 (包括供電、人力等)，與未來相關法規更趨於嚴格。

posts.text: The Dow lagged the bounce, and that tells you what kind of bounce it was. The Dow rose about 3.2% while the S&P rose about 5% and the Nasdaq rose about 6.7%. The money went to growth, not to value, and to the names that fell hardest, not to the names that held up best. That is a bounce led by the selloff's victims, not by the market's steady earners. It does not mean the Dow is broken. It means the rally was about the unwind of the growth selloff, and the value names never joined the trade. When the steady names start leading, the bounce is broadening. Until then, it is a growth bounce, and growth bounces live and die on the next headline. Watch whether the Dow catches up, or keeps trailing.

Across four decades of modern options markets, a 40 VIX has only printed six times.

Five of those six times marked the exact bottom

• 1987: Black Monday capitulation low 
• 1998: The literal bottom tick of the LTCM crisis 
• 2002: The terminal flush of the dot-com bust 
• 2008: The only failure (full banking system insolvency) • 2011: The cycle low before an eight-year bull run 
• 2020: The generational COVID liquidation wick

Friday was the seventh.

The only time buying a 40 VIX failed was 2008, when the global banking system froze. Every other time, it was the trade of the year.

quoted.text:
You are living through one of the rarest statistical events in modern financial history.

Today, the VIX hit 32.

Most retail investors see a 30+ VIX and panic. But if you study market history and derivatives research, a VIX crossing 30 is one of the rarest and most critical macro signals in finance

In normal markets, the VIX lives between 15 and 20. A VIX  above 30 only happens in about 5% of all trading sessions in history. 

• 1997: Asian Financial Crisis 
• 1998: Russian Default & LTCM Collapse 
• 2000–2001: Dot-Com Bust 
• 2002: Enron & WorldCom Scandals 
• 2008: Great Financial Crisis 
• 2011: U.S. Credit Rating Downgrade 
• 2020: COVID-19 Global Shock 
• April 2025: Tariff & Trade War Repricing 
• March 2026: Geopolitical Escalation

What do all of these have in common? Forced margin liquidations and structural repricing.

But don't mistake extreme fear for an immediate green light.

A 30+ VIX can mark a generational bottom (like 1997, 2011, or 2020) or it can be a devastating bull trap if credit and fundamentals are broken (like 2000 and 2008).

The Political Battle Over AI and The Fight To Control America’s Economic Future Before 2028

On September 13, I examined the convergence of political interests, corporate incentives and calls to slow AI development. On November 3, I discussed how an economic crisis could reshape AI policy. On November 11, I questioned the timing of the intelligence revelations surrounding Jensen Huang.

Following Huang’s reinstatement, Hakeem Jeffries is demanding investigations into NVIDIA, Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce, alongside stronger semiconductor export restrictions.

The Political Groundwork

In December 2025, Jeffries established the House Democratic Commission on AI and the Innovation Economy.

In September, Obama privately encouraged making AI central to the Democratic agenda, while Dario Amodei, Sam Altman and Elon Musk expressed support for stronger AI oversight.

Democrats had reason to anticipate a strong midterm performance and develop their governing agenda before assuming congressional control.

On October 29, Democratic lawmakers introduced a resolution opposing taxpayer bailouts following an AI collapse. Valerie Foushee, a leader of Jeffries’s AI commission, was a sponsor.

That same day, the Huang intelligence revelations became public, 5 days before the midterms.

The Intelligence Disclosure

Trump was reportedly briefed in 2025, while Rubio oversaw an intelligence assessment in spring 2026.

My post examined 2 possibilities.

•    Individuals with access to classified intelligence strategically disclosed the information for political leverage.

•    Chinese intelligence sacrificed a potentially compromised relationship to destabilize American AI leadership and semiconductor policy.

Neither theory has been established. Why intelligence reportedly known for months surfaced immediately before the election deserves scrutiny.

Democrats subsequently secured a decisive electoral victory and will gain greater congressional investigative authority in January.

The Economic And Political Collision

Huang’s resignation intensified technology losses and institutional deleveraging. His reinstatement restored approximately $950 billion in NVIDIA market capitalization.

Persistent energy disruptions threaten corporate profitability and household purchasing power. Credit conditions are deteriorating while AI infrastructure commitments face uncertainty surrounding future returns.

Congressional investigations could examine AI financing, private credit, export licensing, electricity costs, corporate relationships and employment displacement.

Established AI companies could benefit from regulatory requirements that smaller competitors struggle to afford.

Political and corporate interests could therefore converge around the same regulatory agenda without any coordinated effort to engineer a market collapse.

The Battle Over What Comes After

If a severe recession develops in 2027, disagreements over corporate bailouts, household relief, AI regulation and responsibility for economic losses could dominate Washington.

Democratic congressional control could influence that response.

Persistent energy inflation could delay monetary easing. Even when rate cuts begin, monetary policy cannot restore energy supplies or make unprofitable AI investments economically viable.

The broader benefits for employment, consumption and investment could take 18 to 24 months or longer to materialize.

If easing begins in 2027, meaningful recovery might not arrive until 2028 or 2029, carrying significant electoral consequences.

Politicians do not need to manufacture an economic crisis to influence its consequences. Huang’s reinstatement may have temporarily stabilized the AI trade, but the larger battle over who regulates the industry, who absorbs its potential losses and who receives credit for the eventual economic recovery may only be beginning.

•   Rokos held $530 million.

Combined exposure exceeded $8 billion in common stock, excluding derivatives.

These positions may have changed, and disclosed options and undisclosed hedges could offset losses. Nevertheless, the scale of their involvement warrants attention.

Following Jensen Huang’s resignation on November 12, the technology selloff intensified. Global hedge funds reportedly lost approximately 4% in November through the 20th, with Goldman Sachs identifying aggressive deleveraging.

If these four funds experienced comparable November losses, their cumulative drawdowns could range from approximately 6% to 9% since October began.

The Prime Brokerage Connection

All four managers have documented prime brokerage relationships with affiliates of JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley.

These institutions provide financing, securities lending, derivatives services and access to leverage.

When volatility increases and portfolio values decline, prime brokers can increase collateral requirements and reduce available leverage. Funds also face internal risk limits that can force portfolio managers to unwind positions.

Relatively modest capital losses can therefore trigger disproportionately large reductions in market exposure.

Why Gold And Silver Could Become Collateral Damage

SEC filings also reveal gold related holdings and derivatives exposure at Millennium, Balyasny and Marshall Wace, while Rokos disclosed exposure to gold miners.

If losses elsewhere create liquidity needs, these institutions could sell precious metals regardless of their fundamental outlook.

Elevated financing costs, dollar appreciation and correlated positioning could amplify the pressure.

We witnessed similar dynamics in 2008 and March 2020, when even traditionally defensive assets were liquidated as institutions scrambled for cash.

Why The Liquidation May Not Be Over

I suspect Huang’s resignation accelerated a deleveraging process that was already underway rather than initiating it.

His reinstatement may relieve immediate market pressure, but it does not automatically reverse accumulated losses, restore leverage allowances or eliminate collateral requirements.

There is no confirmation that these specific funds are responsible for precious metals selling or that their prime brokers issued margin calls.

Nevertheless, their disclosed exposures, reported losses and broader industry deleveraging make them worth monitoring.

The biggest mistake investors could make is confusing speculative selling exhaustion with the end of systemic deleveraging. When institutions need dollars, what they believe an asset is worth becomes secondary to how quickly they can sell it.

Bill Ackman Sounds The Alarm On A Federal Reserve Policy That Could Deepen America’s Economic And Debt Crisis

Bill Ackman @BillAckman raises a warning about a Federal Reserve rate increase on December 9. I share his concern that policymakers may be underestimating the deterioration occurring while relying on headline growth and employment figures.

His argument that geopolitical instability, inflationary pressures and changing economic conditions warrant monetary policy flexibility deserves consideration.

Financial Conditions Are Already Tightening

The rising cost of capital is becoming difficult for businesses to absorb. SpaceX secured financing at 8.259%.

Banks report weakening loan demand and tighter lending standards. Household debt reached $19.1 trillion, with 5% in some stage of delinquency.

Small business Subchapter V bankruptcies increased 43% through October, while approximately $875 billion in commercial mortgages face maturities in 2026.

Meanwhile, GDP benefits from government spending and concentrated AI investment, even as weakness spreads throughout other areas of the economy.

Unemployment near 4.2% fails to capture reduced working hours, discouraged workers, involuntary part time employment and hiring freezes.

Businesses typically reduce investment and hiring before deteriorating profitability forces layoffs.

The Inflation Problem Monetary Policy Cannot Resolve

Geopolitical instability, tariffs, deglobalization, military expenditures and massive AI infrastructure requirements are creating structural inflationary pressures.

These developments do not necessarily reflect excessive consumer demand.

Diesel refining margins near $80 per barrel despite declining crude prices illustrate how supply constraints can sustain elevated costs throughout transportation, agriculture and manufacturing.

Higher interest rates cannot repair refineries, restore shipping routes or increase electricity generation.

They can, however, discourage the investment necessary to address these shortages.

This creates a dangerous policy dilemma. Inflation remains elevated partly because supply is constrained, while monetary tightening weakens the investment and economic activity needed to expand productive capacity.

The Federal Debt and Demographic Constraint

Gross federal debt exceeds 120% of GDP, while publicly held debt approaches 100%.

Reducing these ratios requires debt to grow more slowly than nominal GDP, not necessarily repaying outstanding obligations.

But America’s demographic trajectory makes generating sufficient real economic growth difficult.

The BLS projects annual labor force growth of just 0.3% through 2035, while population aging increases retirement and health care obligations.

AI and automation could improve productivity, but capital expenditures do not automatically translate into widespread economic efficiency.

Higher inflation could increase nominal GDP and reduce the relative burden of existing debt. However, higher inflation expectations could also increase Treasury yields as debt matures.

Persistent primary deficits complicate the arithmetic, even if inflation settles near 3%.

The Bigger Economic Risk

Financial conditions can continue tightening without additional Fed increases. Real borrowing costs rise when inflation expectations decline while nominal rates remain elevated, and a stronger dollar and widening credit spreads create restraint.

Meanwhile, deteriorating household credit, business restructurings and commercial real estate refinancing pressures reveal vulnerabilities that headline economic indicators may not fully capture.

My concern is that monetary policy remains restrictive until credit losses, refinancing failures and unemployment begin reinforcing one another. By then, the economy could already be experiencing a self sustaining contraction, leaving the Federal Reserve responding to economic damage that accumulated long before it became visible in the headline data.

The cost of equity capital has also increased materially with the recent substantial decline in the stock market.

Gold and silver may be approaching selling exhaustion but I am considerably less convinced that the broader liquidation cycle has ended.

Gold recently declined approximately 12%, while silver lost roughly 21%. Despite rebounding 4% and 5% today, they recovered only 29% and 19% of their previous losses.

Recent positioning data also suggest substantial speculative selling has occurred, with silver’s net speculative long position reportedly falling to just 17 contracts.

That supports the possibility of a near term bottom, but speculative liquidation and systemic deleveraging are two entirely different things.

Claims of backwardation, if sustained and verified, could indicate unusually strong demand for immediate physical delivery. However, physical scarcity does not guarantee rising prices when financial institutions are forced to raise liquidity.

During 2008 and March 2020, precious metals experienced significant liquidation despite their appeal as monetary safe havens.

When institutions need cash to meet margin calls, repay debt or reduce leverage, they sell what they can, not necessarily what they want to.

The Bigger Warning Is Coming From Credit and Currency Markets

The Dollar Index above 104, elevated real interest rates, widening credit spreads among weaker borrowers and deteriorating private sector lending conditions suggest financial pressures remain substantial.

I believe we may be transitioning from an inflationary economic cycle toward a much more dangerous credit and balance sheet adjustment.

As leveraged positions unwind, demand for dollars can increase, strengthening the currency and placing additional pressure on international borrowers.

That creates the potential for another wave of forced asset sales, regardless of how attractive precious metals appear fundamentally.

The Refining Market Is Revealing Another Economic Vulnerability

The latest refining data make this situation even more concerning.

The benchmark U.S. crack spread has fallen from approximately $72 per barrel in September to $41, suggesting the extreme refining squeeze is easing.

But beneath that decline, diesel refining margins remain near $80 per barrel, compared with approximately $20 for gasoline.

Diesel margins are roughly four times higher, while distillate inventories remain approximately 15% below their five year average.

That divergence matters.

Falling crude and gasoline margins could reflect improving supply, weakening demand or both. Yet persistent diesel shortages continue raising costs throughout transportation, agriculture, manufacturing and distribution.

Businesses could therefore experience weakening revenue growth while essential operating costs remain elevated.

That combination compresses profitability, discourages investment and eventually threatens employment.

It also complicates the Federal Reserve’s ability to ease monetary policy if inflation remains elevated despite deteriorating economic activity.

Why I Believe Another Liquidation Wave Remains Possible

Silver is particularly vulnerable because weakening industrial activity could compound selling driven by financial deleveraging.

I have greater confidence in gold establishing a durable bottom, but even gold is not immune to a systemic liquidity shock.

A broader dollar funding crisis has not been confirmed, and stabilizing financial conditions could support a substantial recovery in precious metals.

Nevertheless, my concern is that speculative selling may be nearing completion while the larger global deleveraging process is only beginning.

The critical question is not whether investors have finished selling gold and silver because they no longer want them. It is whether the global financial system has finished selling assets because it needs dollars.

Given restrictive real rates, weakening credit conditions, mounting refinancing pressures and persistent energy distortions, I believe another liquidation phase remains a serious possibility.

posts.text:
The Dollar’s Relentless Rise May Be Signaling The Beginning Of A Global Deleveraging Crisis

I believe the dollar’s extraordinary strength reflects something far more consequential than expectations for another Federal Reserve rate hike. The global financial system may be transitioning from an inflation problem toward a credit and balance sheet problem as restrictive monetary conditions collide with weakening growth.

What Robin Brooks’s Chart Reveals

@robin_j_brooks shows the dollar accelerating against G10 currencies while America’s forward interest rate advantage has failed to keep pace.

That divergence matters. When the dollar rises without a corresponding increase in relative yields, something beyond conventional monetary policy expectations is driving demand.

What I think is happening is that elevated real interest rates, defensive capital flows and the unwinding of leveraged international positions are driving the dollar higher.

ING recently reported U.S. 2 year real swap rates exceeding 2.4%, approaching their highest levels since 2023.

When inflation expectations decline faster than nominal rates, real borrowing costs increase even without additional Fed tightening.

The Global Deleveraging Mechanism

Brooks also identified dollar strength against emerging market currencies consistent with carry trade unwinding. Speculative dollar positioning reportedly reached levels comparable to the European sovereign debt crisis.

When investors liquidate foreign assets to repay dollar funding, they purchase dollars. That strengthens the currency, increases pressure on unhedged foreign borrowers and can force further liquidations.

The process becomes self reinforcing.

Dollar appreciation pressures emerging market currencies, tightens financial conditions and weakens global economic activity.

Meanwhile, corporate credit spreads are widening, commercial real estate faces enormous refinancing pressures, business loan demand is weakening and labor market momentum is deteriorating.

The dollar becomes both a symptom of financial stress and a mechanism that intensifies it.

Why Geopolitics Makes This More Dangerous

Energy disruptions involving Iran and the Strait of Hormuz introduce another layer of pressure.

Even as crude declines, expensive refined fuels can sustain inflation throughout transportation, agriculture and manufacturing.

Energy importing economies face additional financial strain while relatively elevated American real yields attract international capital.

The dollar may therefore strengthen not because America is becoming healthier, but because conditions elsewhere are deteriorating faster.

Consider what happened today...

NVIDIA surged following Huang’s reinstatement, technology stocks rallied and the VIX collapsed. Yet the dollar remained exceptionally strong.

That suggests forces extending beyond daily equity market sentiment.

The Federal Reserve’s Growing Policy Trap

A systemic dollar shortage is not yet confirmed. Funding markets have not demonstrated the extreme dislocations associated with 2008 or March 2020.

But the Fed risks underestimating monetary tightening already occurring through real yields, credit deterioration and international currency markets.

It may not need to raise rates again for financial conditions to become substantially more restrictive.

I suspect that the dollar is beginning to reflect defensive capital flows and deleveraging rather than simply superior American economic prospects.

The warning is that the dollar may be rising not because the United States is becoming stronger, but because the global financial system is becoming less capable of sustaining the leverage accumulated during the expansion.

posts.text:
The Fed cannot fight FED.

I joined @FerroTV on @business this morning to raise three important points. 

The first: Gold lost 15% in nine trading days and is up 4% today. Both moves are liquidity. In a squeeze you sell what you can, not what you want, and gold bounced the day the forced selling stopped. 

Today's rally came from Nvidia's boardroom, not from the Fed. A December hike is still priced. This ends when the Fed turns, and the Fed is likely to turn before a January hike, if not sooner. 

The US economy is becoming asset-heavy: AI investment is a third of growth, and it is built with borrowed money. Business spending on equipment and structures is up 1.2 points of GDP since 2021. CoreWeave pays 16% for money. That constraint already binds. A funding spike in 2025 was enough to end QT.

The second point was Oil. I call it Schrödinger's Strait: neither open nor closed. Last week, transits through Hormuz fell 15% and seven tankers were hit. The barrels that get through are expensive barrels, and that holds the floor. Enough of them get through to cap it. So Brent is a range, $85 to $100, and at $90 today it is near the bottom of it. 

We took profits before the midterms and are putting a toe back in. The key is carry and equities: a backwardated curve pays you to hold the barrel, the drillers rebuild the system, and the Munificent 7 oil majors pay you cash.

And third:  FED is Fragmentation, Electrification and Debasement, the three forces behind our supercycle call since 2020. A rate hike reopens no strait and rebuilds no supply chain (Fragmentation). It makes the grid dearer to build (Electrification). It raises the interest bill on a deficit that already pays for guns and butter (Debasement). 

These forces keep commodity prices elevated whatever the Fed does. Higher rates do little to them. However, they hurt an increasingly asset-heavy US economy.

Historically, trading days where the SPX closed up more than 5% (73 times across its full history since 1928) have almost all been concentrated in major financial crises, geopolitical or macro black swans, or violent short squeezes during primary bear market downtrends, and have never occurred during low-volatility, steady bull market uptrends. 

Across all 24 occurrences of single-day gains ≥ 5% in modern US equities since 1950, the following day (T+1) has typically seen profit-taking and mean-reverting pullbacks.

JUST IN: Attorney General Todd Blanche says the national-security call on Jensen Huang was a collective consensus across agencies, and that he has no information on Huang's clearance status

Q: "How did the administration, though, just setting aside the potential criminal investigations, actually make a determination that there was no national security risk related to Jensen Huang? And who, is it DOJ, is it the Pentagon, is assessing Huang's continuing access to sensitive national security information?"

BLANCHE: "How we make that type of determination is, there's a whole bunch of ways we do it. We use the intelligence community, the FBI, the information we know. We talk to witnesses. I mean, that's something that we do."

"I know there's heightened focus on this situation, but that's something that the law enforcement partners and that the leadership in this country, whether it's commerce or treasury, state department, the attorney general, me, it's a collective consensus that we reach all the time in all kinds of different cases, not just in this case."

"And how we determine whether a private citizen has access to information, I mean, there's clearances, there's background clearances, there's information that, depending on the project or the job, they're allowed to have or not allowed to have. So it depends on the issue specifically."

"I don't have any information about even what his clearance status is. But I don't know. I mean, I don't want you to take that as an indication that he is or is not keeping his clearance. I just have no information about that."

posts.name: Peter Schiff
posts.text:
OCIF, the agency created by the Puerto Rico government to oversee banks, appointed a trustee with zero prior banking experience to liquidate my completely solvent bank. What made his job simple was that the bank had no loans on its books and no debt on its balance sheet. 3,370 customers held deposits of just under $67 million consisting of cash, precious metals, and mutual funds, which have since appreciated to over $100 million. The bank had more than enough liquidity to pay every customer in full, with funds left over for me.

Yet after nearly four years and five months, the Trustee will have paid himself more than $1 million to return just $4.7 million to a mere 63 customers, out of the 679 claims the Trustee acknowledges having received. That's less than 10% of claims, representing fewer than 3% of customers being paid less than 5% of deposits.

That amounts to almost $17,000 per claim, or almost 23% of the value of paid claims. His quarterly payments have been increasing over time, with the most recent haul netting him $205,540. At this rate, he is now "earning" $822,160 per year. Worse, there is no end in sight to the escalation. My guess is that over the next full year, he will clear over $1 million.

This is why he has no incentive to pay claims and every incentive to keep the gravy train running as long as possible. Plus, mine is not the only bank he is liquidating, nor is it the only work he is doing. My guess is that this is just a side hustle that nets him many times what he could possibly earn working full-time in a truly private-sector job.

Worse, this is not how much the Trustee has spent liquidating my bank, just what he has paid himself to do it. In total, the Trustee has spent $2.6 million. That's almost $41,300 per paid claim, or 55% of the total value of claims paid.

What makes this so frustrating is that none of this was necessary. The OCIF Commissioner sacrificed thousands of innocent customers purely as a publicity stunt. She lied that the action was meant to protect customers, but the facts show that customers were in no danger at all until the Puerto Rico government stepped in to "protect" them.

1936’da Japonya’nın Hyogo bölgesinde, fakir bir çiftçi ailesinin en küçük çocuğu olarak doğan bir adam, 19 yaşında pet shop’ta çalışırken borsaya başlıyor. 

Bugün 88 yaşında, hala her gün işlem yapıyor ve yaklaşık 2 milyar yenlik (14 milyon dolar civarı) bir servete sahip.

Adamın adı Shigeru Fujimoto. Kobe’de yaşıyor. Lise bittikten sonra bir pet shop’ta işe giriyor. Dükkâna sık gelen bir aracı kurum yöneticisiyle sohbet ediyor, adam ona hisse almasını tavsiye ediyor. Fujimoto ilk hisselerini o dönemde alıyor. Sharp ve petrol şirketi Eneos gibi isimler.

Sonra kendi pet shop’unu açıyor, ardından mahjong salonu işletiyor. 1986’da salonları satıp 65 milyon yen elde ediyor ve tam zamanlı yatırımcı oluyor. O yıllar Japonya’nın balon dönemi. Varlıkları 1 milyar yene çıkıyor.

Balon patlıyor. Serveti 200 milyon yene düşüyor. 1995’te Kobe depremi geliyor. Apartmanının girişi yıkılıyor, tanıştığı birini kaybediyor. Ama devam ediyor.

2002’de, 66 yaşındayken bilgisayar alıyor ve internet üzerinden işlem yapmaya başlıyor. Bugün odasında üç monitör var. Sabah erken kalkıyor, ABD piyasasını takip ediyor, günde yüzlerce emir giriyor. Bazen sabah 2’de uyanıyor.

Geçen yıl bir şirkette yüzde 5’ten fazla hisse aldığı ortaya çıkınca o hisse yüzde 17 artıyor. Yerel medya ona “Japonya’nın Warren Buffett’ı” diyor. Kendisi hâlâ araba ve cep telefonu kullanmıyor. Para biriktirmenin eğlenceli olduğunu söylüyor.

Düşünün, adam pet shop’ta çalışırken başlamış. Aslında o dönemde 19 yaşında, çiftçi çocuğu, ne anlar? diye düşünenler olmuştur. Ama 70 yıla yakın devam etmiş.

Normalde insan bu kadar uzun süre aktif işlem yapan birinin büyük servet biriktirdiğini beklemiyor. Yani sıradan bir dükkan çalışanı olarak başlamış, deprem ve balon patlamasını atlatmış.

Adam o yıllarda gördüğü fırsatı ve sonra da bilgisayarı değerlendirmiş. Nereden baksanız ilginç bir süreklilik.

Wereldkampioen sparen, verliezer in koopkracht

Nederlanders beleggen voor 242 miljard!

Dat is de laatste update van De Nederlandsche Bank. Liefst 242 miljard euro van het vrije vermogen (dus exclusief pensioenen en woningen) wordt belegd. Dat klinkt gigantisch, maar die kwalificatie verdient een flinke nuance.

Nederlanders hebben namelijk nog veel meer spaargeld. Met 660 miljard euro vertegenwoordigen spaarrekeningen een duizelingwekkende 73% van ons vermogen. Aandelen zijn goed voor 19% en obligaties voor 8%.

Die enorme berg spaargeld is bepaald geen goede keuze geweest. De rente is immers structureel te laag, waardoor inflatie de koopkracht van je spaargeld opeet. En niet zo’n beetje ook: over de afgelopen vijf jaar is 17% aan koopkracht verdampt. Met spaargeld op de rekening in 2021 kun je nu bijna een vijfde minder boodschappen doen.

Stel dat de verdeling van het vermogen van Nederlandse huishoudens constant was gebleven. Geen vreemde aanname, want Nederlanders maken al tientallen jaren een sport van sparen. Dan was de koopkracht van het Nederlandse vermogen met 7% gedaald. Een fors verlies dus.

Had je dat spaargeld in aandelen gestopt, dan was je koopkracht met 26% toegenomen. Je had dan wel meer risico genomen, daar moet je rekening mee houden, maar je had in ieder geval geen koopkracht verloren.

Was je zo slim geweest om, zoals wij voorstellen, ook een deel van je geld in goud te beleggen, dan was je nog beter af geweest. Goud leverde, zelfs na de prijsdaling van de afgelopen maanden, over de afgelopen vijf jaar een rendement van 99% op, en dat is dus ook na aftrek van inflatie.

Een portefeuille van 60% aandelen, 20% goud en 20% spaargeld had de koopkracht van Nederlanders gemiddeld 42% vooruitgeholpen. Vergelijk dat met de werkelijke mix en je houdt een koopkrachtverschil van bijna 50 procentpunten over. Stel je eens voor wat je daarmee had kunnen doen.
Is sparen wel veilig? Niet als je meetelt wat bepalend is voor je echte resultaat: inflatie.

Nog niet aan het beleggen?

De dalende koersen van de afgelopen weken hebben je alvast geholpen aan een beter instapmoment.
