posts.name: Michael A. Arouet
posts.text:
When I post about France heading toward a debt crisis, someone always replies, "But look at the US debt." Guess what, France and the United States carry comparable public debt burdens, roughly 119% of GDP for France and 127% for the US, yet the nature of that debt differs sharply.

US Treasuries sit at the center of the global financial system. They are the deepest, most liquid safe asset, the primary reserve-currency instrument, and the preferred high-quality collateral. Central banks, money-market funds, insurers, and institutional investors hold them not merely by choice but as a structural necessity for liquidity, risk management, and reserves. Flight-to-safety demand reinforces this role in stress. That captive, recurring demand gives the United States a wide margin for error.

French government bonds enjoy no such privilege. Non-residents hold a large share (around 50–60%), but this is discretionary demand driven by yield, index inclusion, and relative value within the euro area. French banks and insurers hold some for regulatory or portfolio reasons, yet nothing forces global investors to own French bonds the way the system forces them to own US Treasuries. When political or fiscal risks rise, that capital can leave quickly.

This distinction matters because France has shown little to none willingness to address the underlying drivers of its debt path. Successive governments have struggled with pension costs, and the two presidential candidates currently leading most polls, Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, both campaign on reversing the recent rise in the retirement age and returning it toward 60–62.

Markets have so far more or less tolerated this, helped by the European Central Bank’s residual presence, but tolerance is not structural. Unlike the United States, France cannot rely on a permanent global bid for its paper. If deficits remain elevated and reform stalls, spreads will eventually widen even further, funding costs will rise, and the adjustment will be imposed from outside, through higher borrowing rates, forced spending restraint, or both, rather than chosen at home. 

The arithmetic is not especially subtle, only the timing is uncertain. The second Euro crisis will begin in France, and it will take down the entire Eurozone with it. Prove me wrong if you can. https://x.com/michaelaarouet/status/2117895061711077714/photo/1

The St. Louis Fed Survey Reveals Collapsing Loan Demand As Stalling Monetary Velocity Raises The Risk Of A Much Deeper Economic Contraction

The November 17 Eighth District Economic Conditions Survey reveals collapsing loan demand, tightening credit standards and rising delinquencies.

Examined alongside the November 2 national Fed lending survey and stagnating monetary velocity, these developments suggest the cumulative effects of monetary tightening are becoming increasingly visible.

Bankers Underestimated the Deterioration

The approximate net percentage readings reveal a significant reversal.

•  Loan demand collapsed from positive 11% to negative 30%.

•  Credit standards increased from 6% to 13%.

•  Delinquencies increased from 25% to 28%.

Bankers expected loan demand to remain positive at 11%, missing the actual reading by 41 percentage points.

Next quarter, they expect demand to recover to negative 7%, while standards remain restrictive and delinquencies elevated. Even if realized, this represents less widespread deterioration rather than renewed expansion.

The National Credit Data Reinforce The Warning

The November 2 SLOOS revealed negative net commercial loan demand of 11.7% for larger firms and 11.9% for smaller firms.

Of 12 banks explaining weaker demand, 11 cited reduced investment in plant and equipment, while 10 cited alternative financing sources.

Standards tightened across commercial real estate and every surveyed nonbank financial category. Among banks explaining tighter nonbank lending conditions, 71.4% cited deteriorating current or expected borrower financial strength.

Credit card demand strengthened while mortgage and auto loan demand weakened, suggesting some households increasingly rely on revolving credit to absorb higher living costs.

The Capital Expenditure Disconnect

Regional capital expenditures remain positive while sales, inventories, employment and working hours hover near neutral.

I suspect previously committed AI infrastructure, data center, energy and defense investments are disproportionately supporting capital expenditures.

The St. Louis Fed’s October Beige Book identified strong demand connected to these industries while residential construction suppliers experienced weakness.

Large projects financed months or years ago can sustain activity even as smaller businesses postpone expansion. Rising construction and equipment costs can also inflate nominal expenditures.

Current capital expenditures may largely reflect yesterday’s investment decisions, while deteriorating loan demand reveals tomorrow’s investment weakness.

The Growing Disconnect Between Money And Credit

September M2 reached $23.414 trillion, increasing 5.7% annually.

During Q3, average M2 expanded 6.6% annualized against nominal GDP growth of 5.6%. Velocity declined from 1.420 to 1.417.

Meanwhile, annualized bank credit growth slowed from 6.6% to 5.3%, while loan and lease growth slowed from 8.1% to 6.1%.

If M2 continues growing 5.7% annually while velocity declines 3%, nominal GDP growth would fall to approximately 2.5%. At 3% GDP price inflation, real output would contract.

Is Deleveraging Only Beginning?

Outstanding bank loans and household debt continue increasing, so a broad credit contraction remains unconfirmed.

However, rising bankruptcies, refinancing pressures and tighter lending conditions suggest increasingly defensive balance sheet management.

Nonlabor cost increases registered approximately 53% net versus 32% for prices charged, suggesting potential margin compression. Involuntary part time employment increased by 339,000 in October.

Persistent energy inflation constrains the Fed’s ability to respond.

I fear monetary velocity declines materially before M2 growth slows. If both deteriorate, weakening nominal spending, credit losses, reduced investment and layoffs could reinforce one another, turning a slowdown into a self sustaining contraction despite continued fiscal expansion.

Analyze why such widespread insolvency and balance sheet deterioration are occurring outside an officially recognized recession, what these conditions reveal about the underlying health of the economy and whether conventional economic indicators are masking the true severity of financial distress.

Compare current conditions with previous credit cycles, financial crises and recessionary periods to determine how historically unusual it is for corporate and small business distress to reach these levels without a formal economic downturn. Explain what this could be foreshadowing for credit creation, capital investment, employment, consumer spending and the broader U.S. economy.

posts.name: InvestmentGuru
posts.text: Wednesday's data lands in a thin week, and thin weeks exaggerate everything. October PCE and the second estimate of third-quarter GDP arrive in the morning, with Thanksgiving on Thursday and an early close on Friday. There are three real sessions this week and the biggest data lands in the middle of them, with half the desks already gone. That means the numbers will move more than they would in a normal week, in both directions. A soft print gets bought harder, a hot print gets sold harder, and the moves will not have the volume to absorb them. Do not read Wednesday's reaction as the verdict. Read it as the thin-week version of the verdict, and wait for next week to see what sticks.

So now we have to live in a world where normal people live at the mercy of a small number of irredeemable scumbags who will never ever contribute anything to society and are free to immiserate us at a wildly disproportionate scale, simply because prison is no longer an option (because they say so).

A cohort of 500 career criminals amassed 29,882 arrests including 58 murders, 201 rapes, 55 kidnappings, 405 armed robberies, and 1101 aggravated assaults; 2801 felony convictions, and 1739 prison sentences.

Two reasons why, despite all the chatter over the weekend, it would be very hard for the Federal Reserve not to hike interest rates on December 9th:
Expectations, measured by both market pricing and prediction markets, stand above 90% for a 25 bps hike (see earlier post); and
While this is not the first-best policy response, without the better (fiscal) alternative, the Fed is once again pushed to center stage.
A 50 bps hike, rather than 25 bps, would be ill-advised for both economic and financial reasons.
As to what comes after December, the picture is more complex, given the two-sided questions surrounding the AI spending boom, the fragility of the most interest-rate-sensitive sectors, etc....
